On the ground, something can spook a horse that won't so much as flinch before a backhoe or a pack of roaring Harleys. I call this "horseophthalmology," for it describes a different kind of seeing—not celestial, necessarily, but a vision in which the small, the wispy, the lightly lifted or faintly stirring threads of existence provoke far greater fear than louder, larger bodies ever could. It was Matthew who said that the eye is the lamp of the body, and that if the eye is healthy, the whole body will be full of light. Perhaps, in this instance, "light" might also mean "lightness." Through my eyes of corrupted and corruptible flesh, I fear I perceive mostly darkness—by which I mean heaviness. Yet how great is that darkness, really? Not nearly so great as the inner weightlessness of horses, whose eyes detect—correctly, I believe—the threat of annihilation lurking in every windblown mote of malignant life.

All these years, I have kept wary watch in the obvious places: in bars, in wars, in cities at night and in nightmares, upon furious seas. Yet what has truly sought to destroy me has lain concealed within seemingly friendly breezes, behind soft music, beneath the carpet of small things one can scarcely see. The eye, Matthew tells us, is also a lamp—a giver of light, a bestower of incandescent honey—which I will pour more carefully now upon the paths I travel from here on. What is that whisper I hear? Only the delicate sweeping away of someone's life.

---

It was Matthew who wrote that the eye serves as the body's lamp, and that a sound eye fills the entire body with light. Perhaps here "light" could equally mean "weightlessness." For years I've kept my guard up in the predictable danger zones: taverns, battlefields, cities after dark, nightmares, storm-tossed waters. # Horseophthalmology

There is a particular madness in watching a horse—a thousand-pound animal of muscle and bone, capable of crushing steel beneath its hooves—rear back in terror not from the roar of a backhoe or the snarl of a passing motorcycle, but from a plastic bag drifting lazily across a fence line, or a shadow trembling in tall grass. The great engines of human industry, the loud and the massive, these the horse tolerates with a kind of weary indifference. But show it a wisp of movement, something small and nearly invisible, and you will see terror in its eyes—the whites showing, the whole body coiled to flee from nothing at all. I have come to call this phenomenon *horseophthalmology*: the peculiar science of how a creature sees danger, and how what it sees may have little to do with size or noise and everything to do with something else entirely.

I think often of Matthew's teaching, tucked into the Sermon on the Mount, that the eye is the lamp of the body—that if the eye is healthy, the whole body will be full of light, but if the eye is unhealthy, the whole body will be full of darkness. It is a teaching about perception, about how the quality of one's seeing determines the quality of one's being. A healthy eye does not merely record what passes before it; it illuminates. It makes the body luminous with understanding.

I confess that my own eyes are not healthy in this way. They are flesh, and flesh is corruptible, and what I perceive through them is mostly darkness—not the darkness of ignorance alone, but something heavier, more like a weight pressing down on my ability to see clearly. I do not mistake this heaviness for insight. It is not wisdom I carry when I look at the world; it is a kind of blindness that masquerades as sight, a fog I have learned to navigate but never learned to dispel.

And yet I wonder now if the horse sees something I do not. Perhaps its fear of the small and the wispy is not madness but a correct perception—perhaps within that soft rustling, that barely-visible stirring, there is indeed a real threat, something with the power to annihilate, hidden precisely because it is small. We are trained, all of us, to fear the loud and the large. We build our defenses against the roar of engines, against the visible machinery of destruction. But what if the true danger has always come dressed in gentleness? What if annihilation does not announce itself with the grinding of gears but arrives instead as something so soft, so easily dismissed, that we walk right past it without a flicker of alarm?

I think of my own life and how carefully I have guarded against the obvious perils—the bars I avoided, the wars I feared from a distance, the nightmares that woke me sweating in the dark. These I watched for. These I built walls against. But I begin to suspect now that the true threats were never so considerate as to announce themselves. They hid instead within soft things, gentle things, the small stirrings of life that seemed too harmless to warrant my attention. A quiet resentment. A small compromise. A whisper of complacency mistaken for peace.

The horse, in its trembling, may know something my healthy-seeming eyes have missed. And so I make this vow: to move forward more cautiously, to distrust the comfort of the large and the loud, and to look instead—really look—at the small, wispy, barely-visible things that drift across the edges of my life, asking each one honestly what it might be hiding, before I decide it is safe to pass by.
outputs.L4:
# Horseophthalmology

There is a particular kind of fear that lives in horses—not the fear of the obvious predator, the roaring lion or the charging wolf, but a fear that trembles at the sight of a plastic bag caught on a fence post, or a shadow that moves wrong in the periphery, or a sound too small to name. Ask anyone who has spent time around these animals and they will tell you: horses are not built to fear the large and the loud. Their instincts, honed by millions of years of evolution as prey animals, are calibrated instead to the subtle, the unexpected, the small disturbance in an otherwise familiar field of vision. A horse can stand steady before thunder and lightning, and then bolt in terror from a rustling leaf.

I have come to call this phenomenon, half in jest and half in earnest, "horseophthalmology"—the study of how the eye perceives threat, and specifically how it often perceives threat wrongly, fixating on the wrong scale of danger altogether.

This brought me, in a strange but persistent way, back to a teaching of Jesus recorded in the Gospel of Matthew: "The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness." It is a teaching about perception—about how what we choose to look at, and how we choose to look at it, determines the quality of light or darkness that fills our entire being. The eye is not merely a passive receiver of images; it is an active shaper of the inner life. A healthy eye discerns rightly. A diseased eye distorts, fixates wrongly, sees darkness where there is light and misses the true dangers hiding in plain sight.

This has made me reflect, uncomfortably, on my own way of watching for danger in life. I have noticed in myself a persistent habit of scanning the horizon for the large threats—the loud collapses, the dramatic betrayals, the obvious catastrophes that announce themselves with noise and spectacle. I have trained my inner eye, much like an anxious sentinel, to watch for storms on the horizon: the big argument, the sudden loss, the crisis that arrives with sirens blaring. And in this vigilance toward the large and the loud, I have perhaps neglected the horse's deeper wisdom, however irrational it may seem on the surface.

Because here is the uncomfortable truth I have begun to suspect: the real threats to one's existence—to the soul, to integrity, to the quiet architecture of a life well-lived—rarely arrive as roaring lions. They arrive instead as small compromises. Quiet erosions. Little omissions repeated so often they become habit. A slowly neglected relationship. A small dishonesty that seems harmless in isolation. A gradual dulling of attention to what matters. These are the plastic bags on the fence post of the soul—small, seemingly insignificant, and yet capable of causing the entire being to bolt, to swerve off course, to end up somewhere far from where one intended to go.

I have been standing steady before the thunder while the leaf rustles unnoticed at my feet.

This recognition calls for something like a recalibration of the inner eye—a shift from horseophthalmology's irrational fear of small things toward a wiser, more discerning vigilance that takes small things seriously precisely because they are small, precisely because they hide in the folds of the ordinary where scrutiny rarely goes. Perhaps the animal's illogical fear of the subtle is not so illogical after all, but rather an unconscious wisdom about where true danger tends to lodge itself.

Going forward, I find myself wanting to cultivate a different quality of attention altogether—not the frantic scanning for dramatic threats that has occupied so much of my inner life, but a quieter, more patient watchfulness for the subtle drift, the small crack in the foundation, the little lie or laziness or neglect that, left unattended, could darken the whole body with time. The eye that is healthy, after all, does not merely look for the large and obvious. It sees rightly across every scale—attentive to storms, yes, but equally attentive to the small tremor that, if ignored, becomes the storm nobody saw coming.

# The Long Ride

Matthew had always been "Matthewwho" online—a handle he'd picked up in high school when another Matthew in his class had claimed the simpler username first. The nickname stuck through college, through his first job, through the slow accumulation of years that somehow left him standing in a dealership parking lot at thirty-four, staring at a row of gleaming Harleys under the afternoon sun.

He wasn't sure why he was there. Maybe it was the restlessness that had been building for months, the sense that his life had become a series of scheduled obligations with no open road in sight. Maybe it was something simpler: the way the chrome caught the light, promising freedom in a way his sedan never could.

The salesman noticed him lingering by a matte black model, the kind with deep saddlebags built for long hauls.

"Thinking about a trip?" the man asked.

Matthew hadn't thought about it in those terms, but the question settled something in him. "Maybe," he said. Then, almost without meaning to, the words tumbled out further: "Maybe in the spring. Somewhere I've never been."

The salesman smiled like he'd heard this before—the vague plans of a man who needed permission to want something for himself. "There's no bad time to start dreaming about it," he said. "Where would you go?"

Matthew didn't have an answer. He'd spent so many years being "Matthewwho"—an identity built around absence, around being the *other* one, the one who wasn't first—that he'd never stopped to imagine where he'd go if the choice were entirely his own.

He ran a hand along the leather seat. Maybe in that word was the answer itself: not a place but a possibility. A door left open just enough to walk through.

He signed the paperwork that afternoon.

The Harley sat in his garage for two weeks before he took it out for the first time, engine rumbling like distant thunder, the world suddenly larger than his daily commute had ever suggested. He didn't know where he was going. He just knew that for the first time in years, it didn't matter that he didn't have a plan.

Maybe in was enough to start.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about horses being frightened by small, subtle things rather than loud, obvious threats—use it as a metaphor for hidden dangers in life.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Horses Know

They will stand steady beneath the crack of thunder, beneath the shriek of engines, beneath the world's loud violence—manes unbothered, eyes half-closed in the storm's percussion. But show a horse a plastic bag caught trembling on a fence post, a shadow pooling wrong beneath a tree, the glint of something small and unnamed in the grass—and watch the whole animal become a language of fear, muscle rippling into flight.

This is the wisdom we forget: that danger rarely announces itself with fanfare. It does not always arrive as the wolf at the door, obvious in its hunger. More often it is the quiet thing. The barely-there thing. The word left unsaid at dinner that curdles into distance. The small lie that seemed too insignificant to matter, laid like a stone in the foundation, until one day the whole house leans.

We are taught to fear the loud collapse—the diagnosis, the crash, the sudden leaving. We brace for thunder. But it is the subtle erosions that undo us: the slow withdrawal of touch, the friend who stops calling for reasons never spoken, the dream deferred so many times it forgets its own name. These do not announce themselves. They flicker at the edge of vision, like something moving in the periphery of an ordinary field.

The horse does not reason its fear—it simply knows, in the old animal marrow of itself, that the world holds its true dangers close, disguised as nothing, as nothing at all. Its whole body becomes a listening. Every nerve tuned not to the roar but to the rustle, not to the crash but to the almost imperceptible shift in air.

Perhaps this is what it means to be wise: not to steel ourselves only against the obvious blow, but to learn the terrain of the small. To notice when something in the pattern goes quiet. To feel, before we can name it, the wrongness threading through an ordinary Tuesday. To trust the flinch, the hesitation, the hair that rises without explanation.

For the wolf, at least, can be seen coming.
It is the grass that moves without wind
we should learn, again, to fear—
and the horse, ears swiveling toward some frequency
we cannot hear, already gathering itself to run.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective, poetic meditation that references the biblical verse about the eye being the lamp of the body (Matthew), weaving in imagery of horses and fear of small disturbances.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Lamp of the Eye

*If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light...*

Consider the horse—
how a single leaf,
skittering sideways in wind,
becomes a wall of flame in the wide dark eye,
how a shadow thrown wrong
becomes a predator crouched in the grass,
though the grass holds nothing
but grass, being grass.

The whole body trembling
because the eye could not hold
one small thing
as merely small.

I have been that animal.
I have shied at paper bags,
at silences shaped like accusations,
at the sound of a door
that was only a door closing.

*But if thine eye be evil,
thy whole body shall be full of darkness.*

What temple is this, the eye—
what strange cathedral window
through which the light either pours
clean as water,
or breaks into shapes
that frighten the very legs
that carry us?

I want the single eye.
I want to see the leaf as leaf,
the shadow as shadow,
the small disturbance
as merely weather,
merely the world doing
what the world does—
rustling, changing, passing through.

Not the great eye of the hawk
that hunts every movement for meaning.
Not the wild eye of the spooked mare
who has confused the wind
for something with teeth.

*If the light that is in thee be darkness,
how great is that darkness.*

Let me be the old horse instead—
the one who has seen enough winters
to know the leaf from the wolf,
who stands in the pasture
while lesser horses run,
who has learned that stillness
is its own kind of light,

that the eye, grown quiet,
lets the body rest,
lets the whole field
flood with an ordinary
and sufficient sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of introspective, literary prose that explores the idea that real danger often hides in quiet, ordinary moments—incorporate a made-up term like “horseophthalmology” to describe this phenomenon.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Discipline of Small Hours

There is a word I have invented for what happens at 3:47 in the afternoon, when nothing is wrong and the light comes through the kitchen window at an angle that makes the dust look like it's thinking. I call it *horseophthalmology*—the practice of examining the eye of something enormous and half-tame, looking for the tremor that precedes the kick.

Horses don't bolt during the storm. Any fool can see a storm coming and step back from the paddock fence. They bolt in the stillness after, when the barometric pressure shifts by some fraction no human nerve can register, when the grass is wet and green and offers no warning at all. The danger was always there. It just wasn't wearing a costume.

I think of my grandmother's hands, which were calm hands, steady hands, hands that had delivered breech calves and stitched wounds by lamplight—hands that, on an ordinary Tuesday, forgot how to hold a coffee cup. Nothing announced this. There was no thunderhead of symptom, no herald. Just a slight list to the left, a word that came out sideways, and then the long unraveling that followed. The stroke did not knock. It let itself in through the unlocked door of a day that seemed, by every measure, safe.

This is the practice I keep returning to: the horseophthalmology of my own life, the discipline of studying the quiet moments as if they might, at any second, show the whites of their eyes. Not out of paranoia—paranoia is loud, is dramatic, is its own kind of theater—but out of a colder recognition. The car accident happens four blocks from home, not on the unfamiliar highway where the driver white-knuckles the wheel. The heart attack arrives during the Sunday crossword. The marriage doesn't end in a shouting match; it ends in the silence after, in the years of adequate dinners and reasonable conversation, in the accumulating evidence of a boredom too polite to call itself despair.

We are drawn, evolutionarily, to fear the visible threat—the bared teeth, the raised fist, the dark alley. Our nervous systems are exquisitely tuned instruments for detecting the storm. But we are almost blind to the specific danger of *enough*—enough calm, enough repetition, enough afternoons that pass without incident, lulling us into believing that safety is a place rather than a temporary alignment of circumstances, like planets that will, eventually, drift out of their reassuring rows.

I do not say this to make an anxious person of you, or of myself. I say it because I think there's a kind of tenderness available only to those who practice horseophthalmology properly—not fear, but attention. The willingness to look at the grazing horse, the sleeping dog, the sunlit kitchen, and think: *I do not know what you are thinking. I do not know what you are capable of. I love you anyway, and I am watching, not because I expect the worst, but because I have learned that the worst rarely announces itself with adequate warning.*

The eye of the horse is dark and liquid and gives almost nothing away. This is not because horses are deceptive. It is because stillness is not the same as safety, and we have confused the two for so long that we've forgotten there was ever a difference. The quiet moment is not the absence of danger. It is danger's favorite disguise, the one that fits so well we mistake it for an empty room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical, densely imagistic passage about perception and fear, blending equine behavior, scripture, and a personal confession about misplaced vigilance.
counterfactuals.output:
The horse does not see the world so much as it feels the world's edges, the way a held breath feels a room. Its eyes are set wide on the sides of its skull, granting near-total vision, a panorama almost unbroken—yet directly ahead, in the narrow corridor where the future is supposed to arrive, there is a blind wedge, a small darkness the animal must turn its head to fill. It sees everything except what is coming. This is not a flaw evolution forgot to fix. This is the bargain prey makes with the world: sacrifice the center to keep the perimeter.

I have lived like that. I have kept the perimeter lit and let the center go dark.

Job's God, out of the whirlwind, does not comfort Job with tenderness but with anatomy: *Hast thou given the horse strength? Hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?* The horse in that passage does not startle at the sword; it swallows the ground with fierceness and rage, it mocketh at fear, is not affrighted. It is held up as the animal unafraid, and yet any groom, any child who has led one to water, knows better. The horse trembles at a plastic bag caught in wire. It bolts from its own shadow crossing a puddle. The very creature the scripture calls fearless is, biologically, almost pure fear—a body organized entirely around the possibility of the sudden thing, muscle and nerve tuned like a struck bell to vibrate before the hand even touches it.

Maybe that is the truer reading. Not fearlessness, but fear so total it becomes a kind of grace, a readiness indistinguishable, from the outside, from courage.

I have called my own vigilance a virtue. I have said: I am only watching. I have stood at the gate of my life scanning the tree line for what might come, certain that if I only kept enough of myself facing outward, nothing could take me unaware. But the horse in the herd does not merely watch for itself—one animal's head lifts, ears forward, nostrils wide, and the whole herd's weight shifts before anyone has seen anything at all. Fear is contagious before it is confirmed. I learned to read a room the way a yearling reads a herd: not the actual threat, but the flicker in another body that suggested one. I spent years flinching at flickers. I mistook the mare's lifted head for the wolf.

*I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills,* says the psalm, *from whence cometh my help.* But whose eyes, lifted where? I lifted mine toward the wrong horizon for a long time—toward the people I thought might leave, the doors I thought might close, the small sounds in the house that might, this time, mean something coming. I did not lift my eyes to the hills. I fixed them on the middle distance, the place just past arm's reach, the place a spooked animal fixes on before it wheels and runs. And in all that fixing I did not see what stood, patient, directly before me—in the blind wedge, in the dark unwatched center—which was not a predator at all. Which was only love, standing too close to be seen by an eye built for the periphery.

There is a stillness horses achieve, rarely, called *settling*—when the ears go loose, the lower lip hangs, the weight drops into all four legs evenly instead of poised for flight. It is not the absence of the capacity for fear. It is fear, for a moment, laid down freely, like a coat removed indoors because the room has finally been trusted. I want that. I want to stand in the center of my own life with my head lowered, unwatchful, and let whatever is actually there—God, or love, or simply the ordinary unthreatening air—come close enough to be felt, rather than seen coming from far away and already fled from.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a stream-of-consciousness literary reflection on how the eye reveals inner darkness or light, using horses spooked by small things as a central metaphor, ending with an eerie, quiet image of mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
The eye first, always the eye, that wet aperture through which a person leaks out what they cannot say—I have seen kindness pool there like light on water and I have seen the other thing too, a flatness, a closed door with the lights left on behind it, and you learn to read it the way old horsemen read weather, the way they say a horse will spook not at the wolf but at the paper bag, not at thunder but at the shadow of its own ear twitching wrong against the sun. That's the thing nobody tells you about fear, real fear, the kind that lives under the floorboards of a soul: it is rarely the large thing. The horse has survived storms, has taken the crack of gunfire without a flinch, and then some Tuesday a plastic bag tumbles across the paddock and the whole animal becomes a coiled spring of ancient terror, sweat and white eye and the hooves suddenly remembering they are weapons. We are the same. We carry our darkness disguised as overreaction, as the door that closes too hard, as the flinch at a hand raised in greeting. The small thing arrives and the big buried thing answers it, and only the eye tells the truth of what just happened, the eye rolling white at nothing, the eye that says something in me remembers being prey.

And I think of light the same way—not the grand light, not revelation, but the way some eyes hold a low steady lamp, the kind you could read by on a bad night, the kind that doesn't spook at the bag in the road because it has already made peace with what moves in the dark. That peace is rare. Most of us are still the horse in the field, jumping sideways at nothing, at everything, betraying with one dilated glance the whole private museum of what has hurt us.

And I keep coming back to the field at dusk, how the horse finally stills, how its long neck bends again to the grass as if nothing happened, as if the fright were a story it told itself and has now put down—but the eye, if you look, still carries a rim of white at the edge, a small moon of old alarm that never fully sets. And I think that is what we are, in the end: creatures grazing calmly in failing light, an old fear folded into the shape of an eye, waiting there so quietly that a person could stand beside us for years and never know how close, underneath that dark and liquid stillness, the last spook is always standing in the grass, patient, small, and already visible if you only knew where to look.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
